# RAG, end to end {#sec-m07}

Module 6 built search, and **RAG**, short for retrieval-augmented generation, puts that search in front of the model: it *retrieves* the relevant text, *augments* the request with it, and then lets the model *generate* the answer. This module builds the whole pipeline for Tarkika's return policy, and finally puts the hygiene paragraph, P2, ahead of the FAQ that looked so similar to the question.

## Two jobs: preparing documents and answering questions {#sec-m07-two-jobs-preparing}

A RAG system is two pipelines that share one store (@fig-rag-pipelines).

![The two halves of RAG. Ingestion prepares documents and runs when they change. Answering runs for every message.](/figures/m07/rag-pipelines.pdf){#fig-rag-pipelines}

**Ingestion** prepares the documents: it loads them, cleans them, cuts them into pieces called **chunks**, embeds and indexes each chunk, and stores the result. It runs whenever documents are added or changed, not when customers write.

**Answering** runs for every message: it searches, keeps the best few chunks, builds the request (\see{sec-m03-goes-request}), and has the model answer.

Keeping the two apart helps most when an answer is wrong, because then there are only two places to look. Either the right chunk never reached the model, which is a **retrieval** problem, or it reached the model and the model misused it, which is a **generation** problem. Find out which one it is first, by looking at the chunks that were actually sent. Many teams start rewording the prompt when the real fault lies in ingestion, such as a PDF table that was flattened into nonsense, or a page header that was repeated in every chunk.

## How big should a chunk be? {#sec-m07-big-chunk}

Here is a short return policy with five sections, cut in three different ways by LangChain's text splitters (@fig-chunking). The chunks in the figure are the splitters' real output.

![The same policy cut three ways. Too small, a rule and its exception land in different chunks. Too large, unrelated sections share one chunk. Cut by heading, each section stays whole.](/figures/m07/chunking.pdf){#fig-chunking}

**Too small.** At 120 characters, section 3 falls apart. One chunk says that hygiene items "cannot be returned once the seal is opened", and the next says "The rule does not apply if the item arrives damaged or faulty", which means nothing on its own, because it never says which rule. If search returns only the first of these chunks, the model will refuse a return that the policy actually allows.

**Too large.** At 1,000 characters, the whole policy fits in two chunks, and the first of them holds four sections: general returns, electronics, hygiene and damaged items. Its embedding is an average of four topics, so it is not very close to any one question, and whichever question it does answer, it brings three unrelated sections into the request.

**By heading.** Each section becomes one chunk, because the author has already grouped related sentences under each heading. This is usually the best first cut.

In code, a first splitter cuts at the headings. A second one then cuts any section that is still too long, at paragraph breaks first and then at sentences, and repeats the last 150 characters of each chunk at the start of the next. That repeat is called **overlap**, and it means that a sentence cut in half still appears whole in one of the two chunks. Note that `chunk_size` counts characters here, and 1,500 characters of English is about 350 tokens.

<!-- check: expect -->
```python
from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from tarkika import POLICY                  # the policy, as Markdown text

by_heading = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter([("#", "title"), ("##", "section")])
sections = by_heading.split_text(POLICY)    # one piece per heading

by_size = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1500, chunk_overlap=150)
chunks = by_size.split_documents(sections)  # cuts only the long sections

print(len(chunks), "chunks")
print(chunks[2].metadata)
```

```text
5 chunks
{'title': 'Tarkika Return Policy', 'section': '3. Hygiene products'}
```

Every section of this policy is short, so the second splitter leaves all five whole. Each chunk also remembers, in its `metadata`, the heading it came from, which will be useful for citations later.

Code follows the same principle: cut it by class and function, where the programmer has already drawn the boundaries. The same splitter has a `from_language` option that does this for Python and many other languages.

There is no single right chunk size. Cut where the author cut, start with chunks of a few hundred tokens, and measure the results on your own questions (Module 9).

## Give each chunk its context {#sec-m07-give-each-chunk}

Even when it is cut by heading, a chunk can lose its meaning once it is separated from the document. Section 4, for example, ends with "including items covered by section 3", and a chunk from deep inside a long document may say "the limit is 48 hours" without saying what the limit is for.

A simple fix is to add a short note to each chunk before storing it. A small model reads the whole document together with the chunk, and writes one or two sentences that say where the chunk belongs:

> *From Tarkika's Return Policy, section 4, Damaged or faulty items. This section overrides the hygiene rule in section 3 when an item arrives faulty.*

The note is stored in front of the chunk, so both the embedding and the keyword index include it. Anthropic, which named this method **contextual retrieval**, measured how often the right chunk was missing from the top 20 search results, with and without the notes (@fig-contextual-results) [@anthropic2024contextual].

![How often the right chunk was missing from the top 20 results, in Anthropic's tests. Adding context, keyword search and a reranker each cut the misses.](/figures/m07/contextual-results.pdf){#fig-contextual-results}

With the notes added to both the embeddings and the keyword search, the misses fell from 5.7% to 2.9%, and with a reranker on top they fell to 1.9%, so two thirds of the misses were gone.

The cost is one model call per chunk, paid once during ingestion, and prompt caching (\see{sec-m03-caching}) keeps it low. Every chunk of a document is sent with the same document text in front of it, so that long, fixed start is cached and only the chunk itself changes from call to call. Anthropic estimated the cost at about one dollar per million tokens of documents.

## Fusion or reranking? {#sec-m07-fusion-reranking}

Hybrid search (\see{sec-m06-hybrid-search}) combined the keyword and meaning results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which got P2 into the top two but left P4 in first place. Fusion cannot do better than that, because it only looks at ranks and never reads the text.

A **reranker** does read the text. It is a model that takes the question and one paragraph together, and gives a score for how well the paragraph answers the question (@fig-encoders).

![An embedding model reads the question and the paragraph separately and compares the results. A reranker reads them together, so it can see that "unopened" does not answer "opened".](/figures/m07/encoders.pdf){#fig-encoders}

Because a reranker sees both texts side by side, it can notice that P4 is about unopened earbuds while the question is about opened ones, so a good reranker should give P2 a high score and P4 a low one. Embeddings cannot make this distinction, because each text was turned into numbers on its own, long before the question arrived.

That difference costs speed. The paragraphs' embeddings are computed once, in advance, so meaning search only has to compare lists of numbers. A reranker, on the other hand, has to run once for every paragraph, for every question, which is far too slow for 10 lakh paragraphs but perfectly fine for 50.

Fusion and reranking therefore do different jobs, and one question tells them apart: does it call a model? Fusion does not; it is a formula on ranks, free and instant, used to merge lists. Reranking does; it costs one model run per paragraph, and it judges relevance. A typical pipeline uses fusion to merge the keyword and meaning lists, and then runs a reranker on the merged top 50:

<!-- check: skip -->
```python
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3")       # an open reranker
question = "Can I return opened earbuds?"

pairs = [(question, chunk) for chunk in candidates]      # the merged top 50
scores = reranker.predict(pairs)                         # one score per pair

ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True)   # highest score first
best = [chunk for score, chunk in ranked[:5]]            # keep the top 5
```

`zip` pairs each score with its chunk, so that when the pairs are sorted by score, each chunk moves with its score. Hosted rerankers, such as Cohere's, do the same job through an API.

## Fetch widely, then keep the best {#sec-m07-fetch-widely-then}

Two measures describe any search result. **Recall** asks whether the right chunk is somewhere in the list, and **precision** asks how much of the list is useful. A list of 50 chunks usually has high recall and low precision, and a list of 5 the opposite.

The pipeline gets both by working in stages, with the numbers shrinking at each one:

1. **10 lakh chunks → 50.** Hybrid search, which is fast but rough, aims for recall: the right chunk must be somewhere in the 50.
2. **50 → 5.** The reranker, which is slow but careful, aims for precision: the right chunk must be among the 5.
3. **5 chunks → the request.** The 5 chunks come to about 1,200 tokens, the budget for policy text in \see{sec-m03-budget-every-part}.

It might seem simpler to ask the search for 5 chunks directly. The problem is that any chunk the search ranks 9th is then lost for good, because the reranker can only reorder what it is given and can never bring back a chunk that was cut before it ran. Fetching widely first gives the careful step a chance to find the right chunk. In Anthropic's tests, the search fetched 150 chunks and the reranker cut them down to 20 [@anthropic2024contextual].

## Why the model still makes things up {#sec-m07-model-still-makes}

A customer asks, "Do you deliver to Port Blair?", and nothing in the policy covers it. Search still returns its five closest chunks, which are about delivery in general, and the model, which has been asked to be helpful, may answer "Yes, within 7 days" with nothing to support it. An answer that sounds right but is not supported by any source is called a **hallucination**, and answering only from the sources given is called **grounding**.

Hallucination can happen even when the right chunk is present, if the model blends the policy with what it learned in training about how returns usually work in other shops.

Three defences work together against it.

1. **Instruct.** The system message from \see{sec-m03-writing-system-message} already says: use only the text inside `<policy>`, and if it does not answer the question, say a person will reply.
2. **Ask for sources, in a fixed shape** (\see{sec-m05-answers-fixed-shape}):

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    sources: list[str]     # ids of the chunks used, such as "policy-s3"
    found: bool            # False if the sources do not answer the question
```

3. **Check in code.** Every id in `sources` must be one of the chunks you actually sent. If `found` is false, or `sources` is empty, do not send the answer; send the "a person will reply" message instead, and pass the chat to the team.

Replying "a person will reply" may feel like a failure, but compare what each outcome costs. A confident wrong answer about a refund can mean money paid out wrongly, or an angry customer who was promised something the policy does not allow, while a short wait for a person costs far less.

## When to skip RAG {#sec-m07-skip-rag}

RAG adds a whole pipeline, with ingestion, an index and a reranker, and gives you two places for things to go wrong, so it is worth asking whether you need it at all. If all your documents fit comfortably in one request, you can simply send all of them every time, and let prompt caching (\see{sec-m03-caching}) make the repeated text cheap. Anthropic suggests considering this for anything under about 2,00,000 tokens, which is roughly 500 pages [@anthropic2024contextual].

Work it out for Tarkika, and suppose all its policies come to 40,000 tokens. Cached at the example price of ₹35 per million from \see{sec-m03-caching}, they cost ₹1.40 per question. The cache expires, though, when no request comes for a few minutes, and the first request after that pays the full ₹350 per million, which is ₹14. RAG, by comparison, sends about 1,200 tokens of policy at the full price, about ₹0.42 a question, plus the cost of the reranker. So RAG is cheaper per question, while sending everything is simpler and never misses a chunk.

Which to choose depends on four things:

- **Size.** A few hundred pages can be sent whole, but thousands cannot.
- **Change.** Documents that change daily keep breaking the cache.
- **Access.** If some customers or staff may see only some documents, filtering chunks by metadata (\see{sec-m06-choosing-where-store}) is how you enforce it.
- **Quality.** Answers get worse as inputs grow (\see{sec-m02-text-mean-worse}), so test both ways on your own questions (Module 9) before deciding.

The pipeline in this module handles one kind of question well: a question whose answer is a fact stated in a document. Questions that are vague, that need several steps, whose answers live in tables, or that depend on relationships between things need more, and Module 8 covers them.
